# Topic at a Glance

> **One-sentence summary:** Integer linear programming (ILP) chooses a globally optimal set of discrete biological decisions subject to explicit linear constraints.

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| **Domain** | Assembly, haplotyping, network reconstruction, experimental design, and feature selection |
| **Computational problem** | Select or assign discrete objects while satisfying many coupled rules |
| **Method type** | Exact combinatorial optimization; often solved by branch-and-cut |
| **Typical input** | Candidate edges, variants, pathways, samples, costs, and hard constraints |
| **Typical output** | A feasible selected set/assignment plus objective value and solver status |
| **Prerequisites** | Graphs, linear constraints, and a carefully stated biological objective |
| **Related topics** | [Haplotype assembly and phasing](haplotype-assembly-and-phasing.qmd), [de Bruijn graphs](de-bruijn-graphs-for-genome-assembly.qmd), [dynamic programming](dynamic-programming-in-bioinformatics.qmd) |

# The formulation

An ILP has decision vector $x$, a linear objective, linear constraints, and integer variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{maximize or minimize}\quad & c^\top x\\
\text{subject to}\quad & Ax \le b,\\
& x_i\in\{0,1\}\ \text{or}\ x_i\in\mathbb{Z}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Binary variables are especially useful: $x_i=1$ means a candidate edge, allele assignment, regulator, or sample is selected. The formulation separates three ideas that should be reviewed independently:

| Component | Question |
|---|---|
| Variables | What biological choice does each number represent? |
| Objective | What trade-off is being optimized? |
| Constraints | Which choices are physically, statistically, or experimentally impossible? |

If all variables are integer, the model is an ILP; with a mix of continuous and integer variables it is a mixed-integer linear program (MILP). Both are commonly solved with the same machinery.

# Toy example: selecting reliable variant links

Suppose three candidate links connect heterozygous variants. Let $x_{12},x_{23},x_{13}$ indicate whether a link is retained, and let their scores be 8, 7, and 3. If laboratory design permits at most two links,

$$
\max\ 8x_{12}+7x_{23}+3x_{13}\qquad
\text{subject to}\quad x_{12}+x_{23}+x_{13}\le2,\quad x\in\{0,1\}^3.
$$

The optimum selects links 12 and 23. A real phasing formulation would add compatibility variables and constraints that tie selected read evidence to one consistent pair of haplotypes; it must also model sequencing and mapping errors. The example shows the important distinction: the solver does not discover biological meaning on its own--the formulation supplies it.

# How solvers find solutions

Dropping integrality gives a linear-programming relaxation, where a binary variable may temporarily take a fractional value. Branch-and-bound splits such cases into subproblems (for example, $x_i=0$ or $x_i=1$); cutting planes add valid inequalities that remove fractional regions without excluding an integer solution. Modern solvers combine these steps in branch-and-cut.

```text
candidate biology → formulate variables/objective/constraints
                   → solve LP relaxations + branch/cut
                   → feasible integer solution and bound
                   → assess status, gap, and biological validity
```

An optimality claim requires a solver status and, where applicable, a proved bound. A feasible solution found before a time limit can be useful, but it is not automatically optimal.

# Where ILP helps in bioinformatics

ILP is attractive when local choices interact globally and the hard rules can be linearized.

| Application | Discrete choices | Typical constraints |
|---|---|---|
| Haplotype inference | Alleles assigned to haplotypes | Genotype consistency and parsimony |
| Assembly/scaffolding | Candidate overlaps or adjacencies | Orientation, coverage, and graph consistency |
| Metabolic network reconstruction | Reactions included | Stoichiometry, evidence, and task requirements |
| Feature-panel design | Markers selected | Budget, coverage, and redundancy limits |
| Regulatory-network inference | Candidate edges retained | Sparsity and known biological constraints |

For example, [haplotype assembly and phasing](haplotype-assembly-and-phasing.qmd) can be posed as minimizing disagreements between fragment observations and a pair of haplotypes. Graph algorithms and probabilistic methods are often preferred at genome scale, but ILP can be valuable for exact subproblems, benchmarking, or formulations with additional hard constraints.

# Model construction checklist

1. **Define candidates before optimizing.** Missing candidates cannot be selected; spurious candidates enlarge the search and can distort the answer.
2. **Use interpretable variables.** State their units and biological meaning in a table.
3. **Write each hard rule as a testable constraint.** Include every capacity, exclusivity, consistency, and directionality rule.
4. **Scale objective coefficients sensibly.** Very different magnitudes can cause numerical difficulty and hide the intended trade-off.
5. **Inspect feasibility first.** An infeasible model often signals conflicting assumptions or data errors, not merely a solver problem.
6. **Report solver status, time limit, objective, bound, and optimality gap.** These are part of the scientific result.

## Logical constraints

Many biological rules can be expressed with binaries. If selecting candidate $a$ requires selecting $b$, use $x_a\le x_b$. To select at most one from a group $G$, use $\sum_{i\in G}x_i\le1$; for exactly one, replace $\le$ with $=$. More elaborate logic often needs auxiliary variables and a proof that the linear constraints match the intended semantics.

# Pitfalls and limits

ILP is NP-hard in general. Runtime can grow abruptly with more candidates, weak relaxations, or symmetries (multiple equivalent encodings of one biological answer).

| Pitfall | Consequence | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Incomplete biological constraints | Formally optimal but impossible solution | Unit-test constraints on small hand-checked cases |
| Arbitrary objective weights | Unstable conclusions | Sensitivity analysis and domain-justified weights |
| Time limit treated as proof | Unknown distance from optimum | Report incumbent, bound, and gap |
| Excessive candidate set | Intractable model | Filter candidates using validated evidence or decompose the problem |
| Numerical tolerances ignored | Apparent tiny constraint violations | Use reasonable scaling and verify the returned solution |

An exact solver only certifies the formulated model. It does not validate reference bias, sequencing artifacts, or causal interpretation. Compare predictions with held-out or orthogonal biological evidence.

# Tools and alternatives

Open-source solvers include [HiGHS](https://highs.dev/) and [COIN-OR CBC](https://github.com/coin-or/Cbc); commercial solvers include [Gurobi](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/concepts/modeling.html). Solver choice matters, but formulation quality usually matters more.

Use [dynamic programming](dynamic-programming-in-bioinformatics.qmd) when the problem has compact acyclic optimal substructure. Use network flow or matching for their special polynomial-time cases. Use a heuristic or approximation when the candidate universe is too large and a certified optimum is not required; validate its stability rather than implying exactness.

# Take-home Messages

1. ILP turns discrete biological choices, objectives, and hard rules into one auditable model.
2. A solver's optimum is meaningful only relative to the candidates, constraints, and weights supplied.
3. Status, bounds, and optimality gaps distinguish a proven optimum from a time-limited feasible solution.
4. Formulation validation and biological validation are both essential.
